utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand there are some issues to be raised by counsel. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] And unfortunately ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, regrettably your opening words were lost. If there was anything significant in them, repeat them. Otherwise, carry on from where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It was not all that important. Basically we looked at the notebook briefly, because there was a judgement hearing in the courtroom in another case so we didn't have much time. So the view of all of the teams of the Defence is that it would be good to have a photocopy of the notebook, which we could then use during cross-examination especially in relation to some establishment questions and maybe some gaps about the events between the 18th and the 20th. This refers to some dates. So we would kindly ask to have a copy of the notebook, and also to be given enough time until the end of the day to look at the notebook so that then we could begin the cross-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, my first reaction is "no" to both propositions. The second one is the one of greatest concern. The notebook is a small notebook. The entries are substantially dated. It ought to be possible to assess in a few minutes whether there are any entries of relevance to the issues in this case. The idea that you would need A, a photocopy, and B, the balance of today and overnight to prepare by looking at this one document, it seems to be considerably excessive. Turning to your first proposition, we certainly would be of the mind that if you hadn't enough time last night, because of the other court hearing, to look through the document, that we could have a longer adjournment say at the end of the first session today to give you and the other Defence counsel to look through it. But unless there can be identified in that some material that is of clear relevance to this case, and which would be of -- usefully photocopied for the purposes of the case, then we would be not inclined to the idea that the whole document should be photocopied. You have already been provided, we are told, with those parts which appear to the Prosecution to be relevant. The point of view looking at it is in case the Prosecution have missed some parts that you think are very haven't, and they have. And that's the sole reason for you and the other Defence counsel to have a look at the actual document. So for those reasons, without calling on Mr. Moore, we will consider a longer adjournment at the first break in which you can look at the document with other Defence counsel and then if there are any particular matters arising from that, they can be raised when we return. Is there any other matter? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say a couple of things. I understand your directive and sometimes it means a lot that I'm third in line for the cross-examination, so I don't really need a longer postponement, but I would really -- we looked at the notebook yesterday, and the relevant part provided to us by the Prosecutor starts at page 40. The parts that we looked at very quickly it all seemed quite interesting to us up to page 40 as well in regards names, some establishment matters. So I think that it would be very good if we could get three copies of the entire relevant part of the notebook up to the 24th of November. The notebook begins from November 8th, the day he arrived there, and their preparations during training, there are some establishment data there, which the Prosecutor asked the witness about, and we really need to be informed about that. We did react adequately as far back as January when we made our request in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On Mr. Lukic's submission, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will help in any way that we can. I remained here last night with my learned friends. I could have had photocopying done if it had been asked for. It was not asked for last night at all. The problem that I foresee is a small one, but it will delay, and it is this: That when one takes the document and photocopies it, it must be what's called MIFed. It must have an ERN number, because if there is going to be cross-examination on that page, there should be a reference point for it. Now, if I had been able to do it last night, that wouldn't have been a problem. If the cross-examination can be done on the basis of the natural page number of the page itself, because, as the Court has seen, there is a number, we can proceed without any difficulty at all, and I can have, I hope, the ERNing proceeding on a corresponding time-frame. That's the only difficulty that I would see. There is no difficulty photocopying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When will that be available, would you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In chief this morning, I can deal with the issues actually, what I will do is I will change my evidence in chief slightly. I will deal with the document now, because there is not a lot that I have to deal with anyway. If that document can be released, then I will give it to someone to photocopy. Unfortunately, this morning our case manager has been taken to -- or has had to go to hospital, so we have no case manager. I will get someone from the team to take it to evidence and have it photocopied and ERNed and there should be no difficulty whatsoever for my learned friends to look at the document. There is not a lot of material there at all. It's the ERNing that I would be concerned about on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can cope without an ERN number for cross-examination, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then I wouldn't see any problem at all. So I will deal with the document now. If the document could then be released from the registry, I will ensure that it is taken off into evidence, photocopied, and provided to my learned friend within about 20 minutes, I would have thought. As I say, it's a pity it wasn't asked for last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, once again Mr. Moore is more conciliatory than the Chamber. The witness now, is it, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have the witness now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. You could sit down, if you would, please. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made yesterday, which still applies. Now Mr. Moore will continue with his questions. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, may I just deal then, please -- we were dealing with what I will call the Mitnica evacuation, so I just want to deal with that, if I may, please. You've told us about Karanfilov, you've told us about, as you assessed, 60 individuals in charge of the -- what I will call the prisoners. It's right to say, I think, that in actual fact you made a list of the names of the people who were on that convoy and came into your custody; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you make a list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the duties of a military policeman or police in general is to have the list of the people present so that the next day or whenever planned they could be handed over. So in order to do that I had to do have the list of persons whom I received in order to have that tally with the number of persons that I was handing over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, could the registry please turn up the same number that we had yesterday, which was 0214-7205, and continuing throughout. So can I deal with number 0214-7206?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, would you look at page 50 of your book for a moment, please? We have dealt with 49, we have dealt with 48. Let's just look at 50. What does 50 show, please? 06, please. 206, for the registry. Yes. Have you got that, page 50?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What does this represent, what does this tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the sixth officer who was present in the group that we talked with. His name is Jozo Brajcic, son of Jozo, born in 1955, and I was told he didn't have any particular function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that yesterday. Let us now move on, please, to page 51, which is 207, 208, 209, 210, 211, 212. Can we just go through those simultaneously, please? So that the Court get an idea of exactly what has occurred. So we've got 207, can we go to 208, please? 209. 210. 211, please. And 212. And then conclude, please, on page 213 for the moment. Thank you very much. Now, you have seen the sequence of names that are in your book. Who wrote those names in your book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the names that are here, and that are mentioned in the notebook were written in personally by me. If I can explain, I put the surname first, then the name of the father and then the first name of the recruit. At the end is the year of birth. In the beginning I would write the full year, 1958, for example, in the first, but then later, because of the speed and the cold, I would shorten it, so I didn't put the 19, but only the last two digits, 59, 63, and so on. There are a couple of mistakes where they told me the names in the wrong order, because sometimes I would be told that their first name and then the name of the parent, so there would be an arrow in such cases indicating the correct order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to slightly out of sequence, but I will deal with, if I may, if one looks at page 213, right-hand side, it is the natural page number top right-hand corner, page 63. On page 62, 63, the writing is upright, we go to page 63, it's slightly angled. But there is an entry there which commences dealing with the date of the 18th of the 11th, 91. Can you read out to the Court what that says, and then I will deal with that entry and the subsequent entry in due course. So go to page 63, please. And have you got it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read out what that says then, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins, "Received on the 18th of November, 1991 around 1600 hours at the farm in the village of Ovcara, handed over to Karanfilov on the 19th of November, 1991 at 1130 hours lists given to the KP Dom in Sremska Mitrovica on the 19th of November, 1991, at 1530 hours. Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, Colonel Zaric - guards." The text is written in the Cyrillic script and the names were written in the Latin script because it was easier. I started to write the names in Cyrillic and then I realised it was more difficult for me to write the Croatian names in the Cyrillic script, so then I switched to the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal, you've clearly got a number of names of the people that were taken into your custody. So when you were, say, received at about 1600 hours on the 18th of November, and you cite in the village of Ovcara, there is a reference to "handed over to Captain Karanfilov" at 1130 on the 19th of November. Now, I just want you just to stop for a moment, and go back to the time that you had the prisoners of war, or the detainees at Ovcara. You have told us about how you controlled those prisoners through the night. And you have told us how many people were guarding them. Did you have any members or any persons coming to Ovcara through the night and inquiring about the prisoners themselves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well let me say that it was perhaps normal for them to come to ask whether the prisoners were there, they were asking about how many of them there were, what would happen to them, and so on and so forth. So we could say that it was quite a normal conversation with people in uniforms or without uniforms who came, with ranks or without ranks, who came in the course of the night and asked about them. The usual answer was that we were guarding them, that we didn't know what would happen to them later, and so on and so forth, how long they would stay there. But everything was under control and everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the persons that you referred to as "they." Who are they, who are the people came through the night to ask about these prisoners? Can you please be a little more precise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't be sure, because I don't know. They spoke Serbian, I assume that they were members of the TO or people who lived in Vukovar. People who knew that this group could be there, or that it possibly is there. No one came in an organised fashion following a command or something. They just came on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were any of these people armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in that area there wasn't a single person without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is the answer to that "yes"? Is the answer to the question yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we deal with the uniforms, please. What sort of uniforms were they wearing; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were olive-drab uniforms like we all had at that time, then there were also camouflage uniforms, as well as people in civilian clothing or mixed. They would have some uniform parts and some just civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say if they had any insignias on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And even if they did, I didn't see it. I didn't notice anyone wearing insignia of ranks, indicating ranks. And the uniform was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we're talking about people from the Vukovar TO, how many times did they come through the night? Can you give us a general idea?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they would come from time to time, I was making the list, I left for Negoslavci to secure food and water. So I really couldn't tell you how many times people came, who came, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just see if I can clarify the position when one is responsible for evacuees in the role that you were in as, really, military police. Would it be right to say that there are principal criteria. One, that you have a concern from inside that the people that you are detaining do not escape or cause trouble. And the second criteria would be to ensure that there is no trouble from the outside, that people try and interfere with the individuals who are detained. Would that be a fair analysis of the responsibility that you had that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's just as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would those be criteria that you would apply when you are guarding any persons who have been detainees and taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was necessary to reduce the possibility of escape. Or the possibility that someone outside should help them escape. Or try to help the prisoners in any other way. So both these tasks had to be dealt with efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about the task of protecting prisoners from the possibility of attack or physical injury from hostile forces outside. Is that a feature or a factor in your -- in your brief when you protect individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. At the time it was self-implicit in the area. They needed protection from people who might have attacked them, outsiders. We had outside security, we had inside security, in order to protect prisoners from the possibility of escape or from any outside attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on to 11.30 on the 19th of November? The entry that I've allowed to remain on the magic board, and you say that you handed over these prisoners to Karanfilov. Now, you remember that entry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The convoy that arrived on the 19th of November at about 1100 hours, again there were buses, military vehicles, Red Cross vehicles. These vehicles disgorged a group of military officers bearing a variety of ranks. Captain Karanfilov walked up to me, asked me if everything was all right, how the security detail had gone. I told him about what happened during the night, I told him that everything was under control, that I had drawn up a list which was now in my notebook. Upon hearing this, he said that first checks should be run to see how the prisoners had been treated and then the prisoners should be put on the buses. Meanwhile, I should nip over to the command in Negoslavci and have the list typewritten, which is precisely what I did next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you tell Karanfilov about what had happened through the night, namely the TO Vukovar arriving? Why did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the usual reports you make to a superior officer. Karanfilov, at that point in time, was my superior officer, giving me tasks and assignments. I reported to him on the situation and on what had gone on during the night in terms of the security, food, the lavatories and keeping the outsiders outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with the -- the hand-over itself, why is it necessary to have a formal hand-over from one controlling unit to another?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it in the simplest possible terms, there were 181 people who had surrendered and were received. There were some Red Cross people there and some military officers, and these people had the chance to speak up, to tell everybody whether they had been treated in keeping with the Geneva Conventions or not, whether they had been mistreated by any of the military police members there or any of the JNA members there during the night. Or whether any other military recruits had been allowed to beat them or mistreat them. Or whether on the other hand everything had been perfectly all right. One just needed to check whether the hand-over was smooth and check the numbers too. Just to make sure that no one had been killed during the previous night or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, then with what I will call the convoy leaving Ovcara? Can you remember again in general terms, you've told us about the -- I think you've told us about the Red Cross, but I would like to deal with the vehicles that took the detainees. What vehicles were used? Can you just tell us in general terms, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the prisoners were driven on a bus. Three or four of those, as far as I remember. The military police used Puch and Pinzgauers, all the other military officers were arriving either in Puches or in Pinzgauers. So exactly the kind of vehicles that were generally available to military personnel in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if I may conclude this way: As far as you are concerned, were there any problems, significant problems from the time that those prisoners were brought into Ovcara until the time they were -- and handed over by Karanfilov, and then handed back to Karanfilov on the 19th, and their subsequent removal, were there any problems as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I can say: Whatever problems there were, were taken in our stride and resolved. What Karanfilov was told and what the international factors or agents were told was that everything was all right, that no one had complained about anything, that everything that had gone on during the night had been in keeping with the rules of service and, most important of all, the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say the rules of service, what do you mean by the rules of service? What rules of service control or guide the control of evacuees? Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to say this: The security itself ran along these lines: Some people were standing guard, some were resting and some were readying themselves to take over guard duty. There were guards inside the hangar and outside the hangar. Two rings of security, as it were. The other officers who were also there were commanding the smallest units that there were, from squad level down. Everything that needed to be secured was secured. Things such as food, water, and everything else. Everything that had to be done under the rules was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal then, please, with the list itself. It's a handwritten list, you've told us, I think, that you subsequently went to Sremska Mitrovica with that list. In very short phrases, can you tell us what it was you did with the list and how it was compiled? Well, you have told us how it was compiled, but what happened to it after you left Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was given the assignment of getting a typewritten copy of that list to use it as a document for sending those prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica, Karanfilov sent me back to the command. It was between Vukovar and the centre of Negoslavci. On the right-hand side of the road, between the first houses and the hospital. That's where I first came, there was a warrant officer, a warrant officer second class who told me they had nothing to typewrite this with. He told me to go to the other building where Major Sljivancanin was, and find a typewriter there, which I did. This was another house just outside the hospital to the right. I managed to find a typewriter which I used to copy my list. I took this list back to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic who then informed me that the convoy had already left for Sremska Mitrovica. My new assignment was to try and catch up with the convoy. Should I fail, I was told I should go straight to Mitrovica and hand over the list of prisoners, which is what I eventually ended up doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I want to just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if it's possible for the registry to turn over to the following page number, which is 0214-7206. I'm reading it go upside down, I hope I've got the right one. Let's see if I've got it the right way. Excuse me a moment. Actually, 7214 would be a better choice. Thank you. So it should be 7214. I don't know if it's possible for the registry to hold that particular image and then for the document now to be taken from the witness so it can be removed and photocopied, and I can deal with this page subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if the document could be taken now, I would be extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I sincerely hope that I don't have anything to do with case -- electronic here -- electronic case projection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we please now move on to -- you've told us that you went to Sremska Mitrovica. You've told us that you have been to Ovcara on this one occasion. Did you ever return to Ovcara again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the first security job was finished I returned to Ovcara after my assignment when I was told at the company that we now had a new security job because there was new group of prisoners arriving at Ovcara, that most of the company's people were there already. I drove straight on to Ovcara in that vehicle with the soldiers who were already with me. Upon my arrival what I found there was mayhem. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not just for the moment. May I just deal with one or two questions. You've told us with regard to the Mitnica evacuation, you had notice that an evacuation was coming prior to its arrival. With regard to this evacuation, and I'm going to call it the Vukovar Hospital evacuation, with regard to this evacuation, had you any notice that it was arriving?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had received no announcement of that that morning. No announcement of a new group of prisoners of war arriving, that we should be organising a security regime for. So it was for this reason that I had already left and gone away on a different task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us one or two minutes ago that when you arrived at Ovcara you described it as, "what I found there was mayhem." What do you mean by "mayhem?" Can you give the Court, please, a description of what you found and saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the very same hangar at Ovcara where the Mitnica group had been secured previously. There were two doors being used now for gaining entry. The one to the left and the other one to the right. There were several different groups there, groups of what I shall call prisoners. There were people wearing uniform, wearing parts of uniform, wearing no uniform at all, their heads, arms and legs bandaged. Most of them were wearing something. Moving freely around them were military policemen, soldiers in uniforms and people with no uniforms or with parts of uniforms. So to sum it up, this by no means looked like proper security being provided for the prisoners. This was a mess. Disarray.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, with the time that you arrived on this occasion at Ovcara. I'm going to try and use lighting, whether it was daylight or night or dusk. Are you able to assist us that when you arrived at Ovcara, what was the lighting like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark by this time. One could no longer see. It was too dark to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one was to try and estimate a time when you arrived, would you be able to give a time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I can only speculate. But it would be mere speculation. It was dark already, I do know that. I don't know about the time of day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with the persons who were bandaged, you described it as "some not wearing uniform at all, their heads, arms, and legs bandaged." Would you be able to give an estimate of the percentage of prisoners, if I may use that, or detainees who were bandaged or injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 70 per cent of them. Not that I'm really able to give you the exact figure in terms of the numbers of people there. But once I had managed to establish some sort of order for myself, and they were now standing to the right of the door, so I pulled the rope again. The density of the crowd was not the same as during the previous security job. Now, as to how many of them were wearing bandages and how many were not, this would only lead to speculation on my part. I can tell you what my soldiers told me in passing, not formally reporting but just hints dropped in passing, I was trying to exercise command there to get everybody out of the hangar. I was trying to take all the prisoners across to the right-hand portion of the hangar, looking from the door. So these soldiers were telling me in passing that they had already been categorised, the prisoners, based on the gravity of the crimes they committed against the Serbian population. There was a group of people who killed seven Serbs. There was another group, for example, who had slit the throats of three persons. So now everybody was confused. Why was I grouping them all together, since they had already been categorised, as it were. However it was my belief that all the prisoners should be kept together in one place and I gave an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see any of these prisoners receiving medical treatment during this period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, they were all helping each other out. Even the policemen were helping along those who had difficulty moving. As far as I remember, there were people with crutches there, who were using crutches to walk, and those other people were helping them cross to the other side. As for the prisoners, nobody seemed to be complaining. Everybody just crossed without complaining at all. Soldiers who were not military police officers left without complaining. The only grumpy party, so to speak, were the TO people. They were saying things like, Why are we doing this? Why is this being done in this way? However, they too, eventually left and everything was back under control. Again, it was the military policemen providing security to the right with the police officers and a rope was pulled across. So both security rings were now re-established in a way, and the security regime resumed its normal function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us about the Mitnica evacuation that Karanfilov was responsible when he came and gave them to you on the 18th, he collected them on the 19th, and he was what I will call a designated person of responsibility for that evacuation. Did you make any inquiries of who was responsible for the Vukovar Hospital evacuation to try and clarify what on earth was going on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, you see, truth to tell, I didn't even know at the time where that group had come from. There were rumours in circulation, but I had no officers to speak to. I kept asking if there were any officers around for me to talk to, so that we might work together and set up a proper security regime. No one talked back, however. Based on which I concluded that there were no officers in the area to help me. I seem to have been the only officer in the area at the time. And I managed to establish a semblance of order at least, even if there were other officers around, no one responded. Although I was looking for help, I was looking for someone who could help me with that. Anyone, someone from the TO or from the JNA. I was setting up the security regime, and I was trying to get all of those didn't belong there out of the hangar, but nobody assisted me, no one responded when I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It may seem a ridiculous question, but it is a necessary question. Why did you require assistance from officers at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each officer exercises command over his own unit. I can't exercise command over somebody else's unit. Even if the unit is just a squad. There needs to be an officer in command. I was looking for an officer with whom I might work together and agree on the terms of command, what he would be doing, what I would be doing, what the respective responsibilities were, that sort of thing. I was looking, but there was no response. And things just went the way they did until the moment Captain Karanfilov re-emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course, but I want to deal with other topics that you mentioned and we have as yet not dealt with. You have told us that you had been informed that groups had been categorised in relation to the gravity of offences that they may or may not have committed. What did you mean by that, please? What did you understand by that when it was said to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wish to say is that this was not a formal report. These were snippets that I caught in passing while giving my men orders and while I was trying to establish some degree of discipline both in and outside the hangar with the assistance of the military policemen there. There was a lot of foul language being used and a lot of complaints by Vukovar's TO men. That's what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who had been doing the categorising before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who had been doing the categorising. I was just told that this had been done. And I didn't really take this at face value when I came. People's accounts differed of what exactly had happened, but I wasn't interested in stories. My job was to guard the prisoners, much the same way as I had previously done with the Mitnica group. And regardless of whether there had, in fact, been any categorisation or not, my job was not to vet them for crimes. They were all equal to me, all prisoners of war, and I was there to guard them. That was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you were trying to locate officers, what I will call regular officers. Did you manage to locate any person who appeared to be in command or be responsible for what I will call the Vukovar TO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one responded when I called to tell me that they were the commander of a unit there so we might work together. One thing that was obvious though was this: Whenever I spoke to the TO people, whenever I told them to look one way, to look to the door or to the exit, they would always eventually leave without really complaining. They did make a bit of noise, and they did use a bit of bad language, but that was the extent of it. I did notice, however, that they were looking around, casting their eyes around as if in search of their commander, somebody who would tell them what to do. And this later turned out to be true. They were looking out for two officers who were there, and who were later introduced to me as Vukovar's TO officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us the name of those two officers, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was introduced to both of them the way Karanfilov was introduced to me previously and it was this time that Karanfilov introduced these two men to me. And he introduced me to them, but I don't remember their names. The only thing is what I have already said, and that is that one of them, being the shorter one, moved about much more than the taller person. He was of dark hair, he had a dark overcoat, a goatee, I believe, whereas Mirko, the other one, was somewhat shorter than I am. He was blond. And he moved around much more, and there was another soldier who went around with him, a rather fat person. Later on when they were introduced to me by Karanfilov, it turned out that they were officers. As regards Mirko, his first and last name is here. At the time it seemed to me that he was addressed as Mirko. I believe I had met him on one occasion in Vukovar previously, and I wrote down at that time that he was Miroljub Vukovic [as interpreted] [Realtime transcript read in error "Vukovar"] from the Vukovar TO so that his full name was Miroljub rather than Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the way it came out, but needs clarification. Would you look at the screen in front of you, would you look at top right-hand corner, it's copy from your book, it's 2714. Do you see it up there? Have you got your spectacles. Now, that's a copy from your book can you just tell us what this says, and when it was you entered it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have on the screen is the 73rd page, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if yours is the same as mine. Mine is very difficult to read. Are you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. That's the thing. There is number 2 in circle, Olajnica building number 6 in passing. Savic Momcilo Miroslav, the 11th of February, 1969, Vukovar, Proleterska 2 Street, Vukovar. Miroljub Vujovic, TO Vukovar. Perhaps I can clarify Vukovar Street [as interpreted], Vukovar. Miroljub, perhaps I can clarify further if I need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to try and break it into parts because it's running all together. You have got one entry with a star. Do you see that, an asterisk? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you to read this part out and then wait for the question, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the asterisk it says Savic Momcilo Miroslav, the 11th of February 1969, Vukovar, Proleterska, number 2 Vukovar. Kom. Miroljub Vujovic, TO Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you use the word "kom.", what does that mean, please? Kom. Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Short for commander, komandir or komandant of the for TO Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why was that you wrote that in your book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and the last name next to the asterisk, Savic Momcilo, was a guy from Vukovar this was at a time when I was in the Vukovar barracks. And there was an incident related to this person, and he started causing problems to the units that were deployed in Vukovar. He threatened, he cursed them, he even threatened to set a bomb off to kill many of the unit members. At the moment when I met this person I noted down his particulars and I asked him about his commander and he said that his commander was Vujovic Miroljub. Then I went to see this Miroljub, and he told me that indeed he was a problematic person because his parents as well as his sister had been killed, and that he is under stress. After that Miroljub and I sort of made an arrangement of how to treat this person and I believe it was a rather good one, because there were no further incidents with the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And had you seen this person, Miroljub, before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Miroljub that evening at Ovcara. As regards of Savic, he came another two occasions to my office and we discussed cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I really just want to focus on Ovcara and Miroljub.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you do, could I mention that in the transcript at page 21, line 12, the name you are focusing on is misrecorded. The surname is recorded as Vukovar rather than Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Theunens had informed me of it, but I just thought I would deal with that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we've got that noted and now you can focus for all you wish, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I return please to the incident at Ovcara, you've told us about the TO Vukovar, the individuals who were there, and you said that there were individuals who were responsible or in charge, I should say. Now, are you able, please, just to deal specifically with the smaller of the two individuals that appeared to be in charge. So can we just deal with that, please? Firstly, did you know his name, the smaller person's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the moment I didn't. I believe he was being addressed as Mirko, but I'm not certain whether that was indeed so. I may have remembered that wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But even today when I think about it, it seems to have been a Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What height are you, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 174 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to assess whether this person whom you believe to be Mirko was taller or smaller than you? And please don't guess.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko was somewhat shorter than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal with his build? Are you able to assess it, whether it was fat, thin, or just of average dimensions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was well-built. He wasn't fat. I believe he was of appropriate appearance and weight, and he could move well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was he wearing a uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you think he was a leader of that group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Captain Karanfilov's arrival, as I said, everyone from the group would cast their glances towards him, and occasionally towards the other person who wore a hat. Then, after that, they would do whatever I said. My conclusion was that they were asking for a permission from these two as to whether to obey or not. That was the impression I was under at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the first person that you have referred to. Who was the second person that you saw that evening whom you believed to be in charge or in control? When I say that I mean with regard to the Vukovar TO.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other person was somewhat taller than I am. He wore a black hat, a large one. Quite peculiar. He wore a leather jacket as well, and as far as I can remember, that person had a beard. He was mostly in one place, didn't move around much. He wasn't as agile as Mirko was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us that you saw Vujovic that evening at Ovcara. What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there with the rest. When I issued the orders, they all left the hangar. There was no one inside the hangar apart from the military policemen. And around the building there were many TO members, there was yelling, cursing. Because they wanted to stay there. And in order to relax the tension, I allowed them to go in, in small groups, to walk by the rope to see who was there, and then to leave. Once outside, they usually resorted to cursing, they would comment on whom they recognised and whom they didn't. Whether this or that person killed someone, they were explaining things to each other and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, how would you describe the atmosphere in that hangar with the TO Vukovar behaving the way that they have done? Can you paint a picture for us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind the moment as of which the control was re-established, it means that there was no one there anymore who wasn't supposed to have been there, apart from the people that we would let in occasionally. The situation outside was quite unchanged. They were angry, cursing. And once they would leave the hangar, they explained things to each other. You know, that guy was from that part of Vukovar, and he used to live there, he killed this or that person. And it just increased the tension among the Vukovar TO members, because they had members of their family or relatives killed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have said that they were saying what they would do. What sort of things were they saying they were going to do to the people inside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one spoke directly to me. No one tried to tell me to do anything, but they were talking among themselves in small groups, and one can -- could overhear that. They were quite loud, they cursed a lot. They were explaining to each other whom they recognised inside, where that person used to hide, who did what to whom. No one addressed me directly, trying to get me into doing anything, but they simply discussed this among themselves. They weren't saying anything along the line of wanting to kill anyone, but they were simply cursing the prisoners, explaining to each other what each prisoner did previously. Just to clarify, perhaps, in the Serbian language there are quite a lot of curses, rough ones too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it may surprise you that not everybody is a sensitive individual, and I suspect we are all rather hardened. Would you tell us, please, the sort of curses that were being said outside the Ovcara hangar; would you mind? That won't offend you too much?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember everything that was said. Well, those are nasty swear words. To us they appear rather ordinary because there was nothing to indicate that something could take place later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just examine that for the moment. How many people did you have, how many soldiers did you have in place at that time for the security of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 15 and 20 policemen there. I came in a Pinzgauer, and so there were two more policemen with me. Altogether around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you told us that for the Mitnica evacuation there were something like 60 individuals protecting them. Now, this was a larger group by approximately 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe my learned friend is trying to suggest an answer to the witness when the witness was explaining yesterday that the Mitnica group was at any given point secured by 20 soldiers, and that it lasted throughout the night, 15 to 20. Now a suggestion is attempted that the number was -- of the policemen was such, but the witness only mention the number as regards the Mitnica group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You don't need it, Mr. Moore. The group guarding the previous night was the larger number you used. The fact that only 15 to 20 might have been detailed at a particular time is a different issue from the number that were there and available. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that this group was a larger group. Are you able to assist the Court in the following way: Do you know if there had been any concern expressed by anyone about whether there were enough soldiers on the ground to protect this group adequately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, I didn't find a single officer at the moment with whom I could talk to. There were the 15 to 20 policemen at my disposal, and I had to do with the people I had. Therefore, there weren't enough of them to put together the second and the third shift. That was the number of people I had to use for the rest of the night as well. To provide security at low temperatures for the entire night, that was a difficult thing to do for them. They had to secure the prisoners both inside and outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Vojnovic at any time at Ovcara that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the moment I arrived at Ovcara until the moment I left, I didn't see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you had -- that you saw Karanfilov that day later on. I want to deal with that area of your evidence. When did you next see Karanfilov on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Karanfilov arrived at a certain point to the hangar. I told him about the situation that I found there, I told him about the things I undertook, and I reported the same way I used to report my -- my superiors as regarded the Mitnica group. This officer was someone that I coordinated with before, and I was supposed to carry on. Therefore, I informed him on the situation and reported of the measures undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to again try and work at time. You said that you arrived, that it was dark and it was difficult to assess time. How long had you remained at Ovcara before seeing Karanfilov arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific, but I believe from the moment I arrived until the moment I left, that period lasted two hours at the most. Perhaps I spent another half an hour with Karanfilov, so it may have been an hour and a half between the time I arrived and the time when Captain Karanfilov arrived. But I'm just trying to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had you been told that Karanfilov, firstly, was involved with this evacuation prior to his arrival?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I have explained, there was no officer there with whom I could speak so that I could learn that some people were there from the Vukovar Hospital. At the moment when Captain Karanfilov arrived, he told me these people were from the hospital and that an arrangement was made between the JNA and the Vukovar TO that the Vukovar TO was to take control of the security of the building and the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When he came -- you have already told us he didn't come along -- I will let the interruption proceed before I start my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness said that he was told that the civilian authorities were to take control of the town of Vukovar. I believe that was something the witness stated, and it wasn't recorded in the transcript. Perhaps it could be clarified by my learned friend. I apologise. I was being corrected by my colleagues. The witness stated that the TO was to take control of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with the conversation that you had with Karanfilov. There seems to be some confusion. Please disregard anything you have heard said in your own language and just deal with the evidence that you remember. So can I deal, please, with Karanfilov. What was it that Karanfilov said to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have explained myself well, but Karanfilov told me that there was a meeting and that the JNA reached an agreement with the Vukovar TO that the TO was to take control. I may have misspoken the first time, and maybe the things went in different sequence, but Captain Karanfilov was explaining things to me that based on the agreement the TO of Vukovar was take over the security of the prisoners. That's the way he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I thought you also told us that Karanfilov had said that the prisoners had come from the hospital. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember from where I'm sitting now, I had a notion of what was taking place here, and this was clarified to me further, but I don't know whether in those exact words. That's what was given to me by way of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the other thing was that there had been an agreement between the JNA and the TO Vukovar that the TO Vukovar would take charge of the prisoners. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told there was a meeting. I don't know at what level, or where. It may have been mentioned but I don't remember. I was told that the Vukovar TO was to take over Vukovar, as well as the prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, the civilian authorities -- I apologise. Maybe I manage to clarify somewhat. Civilian authorities were being established, and they were supposed to take over the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the purpose of my intervention is because of a reference at page 28, line 9. Is this conversation with Captain Karanfilov on the 19th or the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I thought I had posed the question, which was on 28/8, which I said that you saw Karanfilov that day, later on, because he had said that in evidence. I want to deal with that area of your evidence. When did you next see Karanfilov on the 20th. So I specifically referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we have moved to the 20th from the 19th. That was the point of my inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have never been on the 19th. I said in actual fact -- well, I understand now exactly what Your Honour's question relates to. I will take the witness back to clarify that. Because I referred to -- that he had been to Ovcara twice. I will ask him when it was the second time. What date that was. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then we will break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, you went to Ovcara a second time. Do you know what date that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Such things as dates and the time of day seemed irrelevant to me at the time. What I do know, is because my memory was jogged during all the investigations and everything, that the Mitnica group was on the 18th and the 19th, and what I'm talking about now was happening on the 20th. I don't think I ever spoke about anything else happening on the 19th except for the hand-over of the POWs from Mitnica, or rather their transport to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you refer to this incident, what I will call the Vukovar Hospital incident, you're referring to the 20th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The evening of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour wanted to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where was -- did you spend the evening of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should talk about that too. Upon my return from Sremska Mitrovica there was a murder in another unit, so I went there to secure the crime scene until an on-site investigation was carried out. So I was outside Negoslavci, and the next day, on the morning of the next day, I drove to Njemci, and once I had left Njemci I drove back to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, we will have a break until 11.30. And I see that there may be photocopies, and that will allow some opportunity for that to be examined. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the evening of the 20th, please. Karanfilov, you've told us that he arrived with various individuals and had a conversation with you. Did you expect to see Karanfilov that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no idea who would be turning up, or if anyone would at all. It was logical to expect though that one of the officers would be there to see how the security regime was going, and to see if everything was going according to plan. So in a way, you might say I expected one of the officers to turn up, and Karanfilov did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what he said to you, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I reported to him, and I informed Captain Karanfilov about everything that had gone on, about everything that I had done and what the situation was. He again told me that there had been a meeting between the JNA and the Vukovar TO. He said an agreement had been reached for the TO Vukovar to take charge of the town, as civilian authorities, and that the prisoners would be handed over to the Vukovar TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you hand the prisoners over to Karanfilov when he said that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The next stage was outside the hangar. There was another conversation between Captain Karanfilov, myself with the big hat, and Mirko. Karanfilov introduced me to the Vukovar TO people, he introduced them to me and said that the Vukovar TO would now be taking charge of the prisoners' security, saying that I was to pull my unit back, or out. What I asked the Vukovar TO people is if they had a sufficient number of men to perform all these security tasks. The answer was in the affirmative. We exchanged greetings, I took leave of them and took all the necessary measures to prepare my unit for heading back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to interrupt my colleague. Page 32, line 25, the witness said, "I was expecting one of the officers, but whether it was Karanfilov or not..." The interpretation was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I'm silent, I'm leaving it to you whether you need to do anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The only thing that concerns me is one is trying to get a witness to give evidence in a flowing way. There are interruptions, I'm sure it is with the best motives. There seems to be a problem with interpretation that go to crucial issues and it is very unfair and very undesirable. I don't know what I can submit about it. I rely on the goodwill of my learned friends and their honesty which of course is beyond any doubt at all, but it does cause concern. I will carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You said, or you asked the Vukovar TO people if they had had a sufficient number of people or men to perform all these security tasks. I want to deal with that particular question. Now, with Mitnica you had approximately 175 people who were detained, and about 60 individuals in -- guarding them in some capacity. Are you able to assess or were you able to assess how many people would have been required to properly protect these detainees? That's outer ring, inner ring, and groups who are staggered in relation to their time on guard.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should repeat what it was that I did. What I assumed would be logical for that sort of a security regime in a different group under similar conditions under which I welcomed the Mitnica group. I expected about 60 soldiers, which was realistic. They could take turns also because of the weather conditions that prevailed. I didn't see or I didn't know how many men they had at the time. That's why I asked them whether they had sufficient men to set up an appropriate security regime. I was thinking that if it was necessary the military police company should join and be under their command, and I meant Captain Karanfilov and Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. That was what my question to them was about when I asked them if they had sufficient men to set up a security regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What number of men did you have in mind as being sufficient to protect this larger group of detainees?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, about 60 soldiers. That would have constituted a minimum. The more soldiers, the easier it is to set up a security regime. Because instead of taking two or three-hour shifts, we could have had one or two-hour shifts, had we had a greater number of men at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you subsequently then hand over the prisoners as a result of the assurances you were given?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once our conversation was over I handed out the assignment to have the unit prepared for our return to Negoslavci. The military policemen came out of the hangar and got into our vehicles and we just drove off to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you drove off, what happened to Karanfilov? Did he leave with you, or did he remain? Can you assist us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the vehicles were ready to go, and the policemen were in the vehicles, I took leave of Karanfilov and the Vukovar TO officers. I got into my vehicle and I left. And they all remained beside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you left Ovcara in your vehicles, what had you believed would happen to the detainees who were then be controlled by the Vukovar TO and Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't quite understand what you're asking me here. However, you receive an assignment from your commander, you complete it or you don't. Then you receive another assignment. This is perfectly normal. I received an assignment telling me to pull my unit out, because another unit would be taking over the security, would be taking charge of the security of the prisoners. This struck me as something that was perfectly normal. I wasn't thinking about what would happen next. I was happy in a way, because I thought to myself it wouldn't be me and my soldiers freezing throughout the night, but a different set of soldiers. In terms of the cold, it was actually a pleasure to leave Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You use the word "assignment." What do you mean, assignment? How does that compare with "order", receiving an order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an order is something that I have to do. An assignment is something that I need to plan. I'm trying to extemporise here in terms of phrasing. When there is an assignment I have to give it some thought, it takes some planning. An order is an order. He ordered me to take my unit away from there. There was nothing for me to think about. The military police company was now leaving, and handing over the security to someone else. And we were supposed to be on our way back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you returned to Negoslavci did you see Colonel Vojnovic there or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can no longer be certain whether I saw him or not. Maybe I just reported to the duty officer, I'm not sure if he was there or not. I reported to the duty officer saying that we were now back to our previous assignment, that we were no longer at Ovcara. Whether Vojnovic was there or not is really not something that I can now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember the date when you actually left the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have got the dates mixed up, but I think it was on the 23rd. This date is the date my children were born, and that's why it remains etched in my memory. I think it was on the 23rd that we got a transfer from Negoslavci to the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Vukovar itself; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, from the 23rd of November, when we got our unit across to the barracks, until the 15th December, 1991. It was on the 15th of December that I left Vukovar and returned to Kragujevac. But as far as I know the unit itself remained until the 15th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will deal with that topic with other witnesses, but I want to deal with the one area, and it is this: Whilst in Vukovar, did you ever hear any rumours that the prisoners at Ovcara had either been mistreated or killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when, at which point in time there were rumours circulating, all sorts of rumours. Someone was killed, someone wasn't killed, someone was shot, someone wasn't shot. Not only in relation to that group of people but all other problems. This was hearsay and soldiers were telling stories. But nobody took this seriously. I did not at any point in time receive any official reports from any of the officers indicating that that particular group of POWs had been killed or that measures were to be taken in that respect. I heard nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with that topic, if I may. Here you are, you're military police, you are in the Vukovar area until, I think, the 15th of January. Did you at any time, were you ever requested to make inquiries or to investigate the possibility of atrocities occurring at Ovcara on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until the 15th of January, I was there until the 15th of December. Nothing was said officially at any time about anything happening at Ovcara on the 20th, nor did anyone request the military police company to get involved in terms of discovering any crimes or in terms of assisting the military investigating magistrate with discovering any possible crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the period until the 15th of December. You leave the area, but clearly you were a unit that was involved with regard to the Ovcara evacuations. Did you at any time, after the 15th of December, receive any inquiry or were you requested to inquire about the atrocities at Ovcara? This is when you were away from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Officially no one ever asked me about it. Not before 1998, or thereabouts, when Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic called me over and asked me if I was willing to talk to him, and General Vasiljevic about this. The general came to Kragujevac, we went to a restaurant, and talked about this. This was the first time that I talked to anyone, but this was off the record, that I talked to anyone about it. I was later summoned by the military court to give a statement. I gave a statement to the military court. There were later statements and trials that I was part of. I gave about two statements or I testified twice in Belgrade, once in Novi Sad, also at the war crimes tribunal in Belgrade, and I don't quite remember where else. Needless to say, I also gave a statement to investigator Vladimir Dzuro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my fault. I should have made application for this witness's diary to be made an exhibit. But I would only make -- well, at this moment I will make an application for the diary as a whole. It may well be my learned friends wish to modify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the whole diary being received in evidence? There is not. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 432.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence assumed that the whole notebook would be tendered and that is why it was necessary for us to obtain the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. First of all, I would like to ask you one thing. We both use the same language, so please make a short pause after each of my questions before you start answering, so that the interpreters may be given adequate time to interpret both my question and your answer and so that we may have an accurate record of these proceedings. You testified in chief about how your unit was mobilised in 1991. You mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic, who was your superior. What was his position, and was he your superior while you were in Kragujevac as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic was an officer of the 80th motorised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, presumably brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's possible he worked for the corps as well. I'm not sure where he belonged, technically speaking. I know that everything about the setting up of the military police company in terms of manpower, in terms of preparation, in terms of the drills that we had back in 1991, when through him. At the time of the last mobilisation callup, Lieutenant-Colonel Jevtic was with us, or rather with me all the time. He was with me in Smederevo, he came to Negoslavci with me, and then after that he went back. I'm not sure if he, technically speaking, belonged to the 80th motorised or to the corps or perhaps a third unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned the corps. Let's clarify this. Are we talking about the 24th Corps, the corps that the 80th Motorised Brigade was part of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic the chief of security for the brigade or the corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic worked with me throughout. He was the security organ in charge of us. Whether establishment-wise he belonged -- or rather his office was where the corps was, and that's why I'm slightly in two minds because of the location of his office whether he was formally part of the corps or whether he only belonged to the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you say, he was competent for your unit as one of his security assignments, did he only deal with the issues pertaining to security or whether he worked on counter-intelligence tasks as well, that he belonged to that group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a reserve captain, so I was supposed to have an officer, a superior who would issue assignments to me, and that would be the commander or someone from the security organ. That sufficed to me, and everything else was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained your arrival to the area of Negoslavci, and that in early November you reported to your unit's command, and they assigned you a location to be billeted at in Negoslavci. Concerning the tasks of your unit as a military police company, did you also organise a facility to be used as a detention facility for soldiers, was that one of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that afternoon, when I arrived there, the sequence of events was the following: First we need to remove the vehicles from the street, we needed to camouflage the vehicles, we needed to prepare accommodation for those soldiers who were not on duty, then we needed to secure the unit, meaning to establish guard points in front of the facility where the unit was, then to organise night guards, and the first and foremost task was to secure an open passage between Negoslavci and Vukovar. There was a check-point established there with some people who provided security. And we also needed to replace the soldiers who were providing security for the commander, for the past few days. Whether during that afternoon or maybe the next morning, well there was a cellar in that building. I don't know whether we sealed it off the previous evening, making it a detention facility, or whether it was something we did the next morning, I don't know. Perhaps if I went through the whole exercise it would take a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That won't be necessary. I wanted to ask you something else. You have explained already how you organised things at the place where you were accommodated. You had your own deputy within your unit as well as two platoon commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember their names exactly, though. Mika Pavlovic was a company officer, I believe. They were not there -- all of them there at the time of our arrival. They arrived successively. So if there was a reserve officer who was supposed to be a platoon commander was missing then I had to appoint someone to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was your deputy commander of the military police company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his name. I think he was from -- no, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your military company there was a traffic police platoon. What were their tasks, and do you remember how many vehicles they had at their disposal, as well as how many men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A constant problem was that we were always being short of people. Another platoon was extracted from the unit in Smederevo and was attached to the Operations Group North. As for the traffic police platoon, they provided security during the movement of the unit, and they directed the unit. As concerns Vukovar itself, since we were short of people, we -- and we called these men the traffic men, I began using them for military police tasks. When they were not securing the movements of the unit, they were assigned tasks of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember who was platoon commander of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Traffic police is tasked with securing or following the column as the unit is moving within the operations zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to Negoslavci these policemen checked vehicles, they secured exit and entry, but they were not carrying out only the tasks that they had been prepared to carry out, but they needed to do whatever I told them. Perhaps I can explain further how I organised the company, but that would take time. But I had to carry out all the tasks necessary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move to a different topic. I just wanted to see what the role of the traffic police unit was. We may return to the topic yet at a later stage. You probably know that at a certain point the 80th Motorised Brigade was assigned an operations zone or area of responsibility, including Jakubovac, Grabovo and Ovcara. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember having been informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A military police unit within a staff or location command is tasked with providing security, order, military detention facility as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Between the 16th of November and the 20th November did you receive any instructions from the three people mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, but they didn't get the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- of tasks regarding -- there is a problem with the transcript. Between the 16th of November and the 20th November, did you receive any instructions from Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic or Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic or Captain Dragi Vukosavljevic concerning the carrying out of tasks of security, providing order and discipline and securing the military detention or prison in the area encompassing Negoslavci, Grabovo, Ovcara, and Jakubovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided I understood your question, I believe you asked me whether I received orders directly from them. I don't remember that. There was telephone communication, or communication via courier. I could intervene in the units who were in the area concerning various things. But I was charged with regular military police tasks, therefore there was no need for them to issue any orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
