In your testimony in chief you stated that together with the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade and some other officers on the 18th of November, 1991, you tried to locate a facility suitable for accommodation of prisoners and their arrival was announced to your unit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We have feedback. Apart from Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic and yourself, were there any other officers trying to locate a facility suitable for the accommodation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember who there was exactly. There were usually officers and soldiers who were not on duty at the time. They would be tasked with doing that. But I don't remember the names of the actual people who went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained how you managed to locate that facility and how you ordered for it to be prepared to receive the prisoners, and you have explained the arrival of the first group of prisoners escorted by Captain Karanfilov. You have also explained the way you noted down the names and particulars of the prisoners. I'm interested in one of your entries on page 48, it says, "Elementary school, Sremski front, from Sid, Captain Karanfilov." You explained that you were told by Captain Karanfilov that that was the place where he would spend the night between the 18th and the 19th, and that you could find him there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is that school, Sremski front in Sid a place where the security centre of the 1st Military District was, as well as the counter-intelligence group for the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srijem; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know where that was. I only said what was told to me, and he said that I could find him during that night, but as to whether he was accommodated there throughout, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he give you any telephone number or did he simply tell you where the elementary school in Sid was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no telephone number. Had I been given one, I would have noted it down. But if we had a field phone I don't know for how long that worked, but I didn't try to talk to him on the phone. I could always dispatch a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand your answer, you didn't ask Captain Karanfilov what his tasks were in Sid, you said yourself that he was one of the senior officers of security within the operations group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I proceed? I'll try to clarify and to be precise. When I saw Captain Karanfilov for the first time, there was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic as well. He introduced Captain Karanfilov in the military sense of the word. He said what his name was, what his function and duties were, and his assignments. And he introduced me to Karanfilov as the military police company commander, who was to be issued with tasks from Captain Karanfilov. I didn't remember the whole thing, of course. But only the points of interest to me at the moment. And that was that there was such a person as Captain Karanfilov who was to manage the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in chief you described the operation on the 18th and the 19th in the morning. I believe you said that when securing the group of prisoners you had shifts of 15 to 20 guards and that those shifts took turns and there were some people who were off duty at any given point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that Captain Karanfilov came in the morning and after he checked the situation he told you that the list you have compiled in the meantime should be typed in Negoslavci, and you have already explained how you went about doing that. I'm interested in the following: It can be found in your notebook concerning the 19th of November regarding Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic and Captain Zaric, and the entry states "the guards". Was there someone present at the place where you were typing the list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned this before, but I will now. In the building where I was told Sljivancanin was, and that was immediately in front of the hospital, the list was typed by a lieutenant-colonel in charge of information, I believe. As we were typing the list he had to interrupt the typing on several occasions because he had other routine tasks and typing to do. So he was in charge of that within the command as well. He had the only typewriter that could be used, and we used, of course, that typewriter. He was actually doing the typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These surnames that I mentioned from your notebook, do you know where you met these people, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, Captain Zaric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly who they are, and I cannot remember how we met, but they probably were people who were in Mitrovica who had actually escorted the prisoners. I think it's in the context of that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained to us how, after the list was typed, you went to Sremska Mitrovica where you handed the list over. Do you remember whom you gave the list to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived there somebody in uniform came out, introduced himself as the prison warden commander. I asked whether everyone had arrived, whether the numbers tallied. He was expecting the list in a way, because he was told it should arrive, and he -- I handed over the list. And that's how long I stayed in the prison. Actually in that room in the prison. I didn't see the prisoners in Sremska Mitrovica, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: They had already been admitted to the prison facility by the time you got there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they had already been admitted. In any case, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And this happened at around 1530 on the 19th of November 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that you returned to Negoslavci. Can you tell us when you arrived and who did you report to when you came?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I don't recall the time of arrival. The driver and I came back alone, I don't know what time we came back. All I know is that in the course of the night we had another intervention and so we were really getting upset because we were wondering if there would be a moment when we could actually have some rest. I guess it's just in the nature of police work to be moving all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned to Negoslavci did the security officer or officer on duty inform you that your unit was supposed to receive a new group of prisoners, about 200 of them, that was supposed to be taken out of the Vukovar Hospital sector the following day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody informed me about anything in terms of an expected new security or guard task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to look at the war diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade before now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit 375, please. This is page -- this is actually the entry for the 19th of November at 1800 hours. In English it's page 10, and it's number 17664211825. Could we please look at the entry for the 19th of November at 1800 hours. Thank you. I'm going to read, and then you can perhaps follow. "In the early morning hours the captured Ustashas were taken to the Sremska Mitrovica prison. Combat activities in the sector around the hospital. Surrender of remaining ZNG forces and MUP is expected, approximately 200 of them, and" -- so there was an order to be ready for -- to be ready to prepare security for these prisoners. Do you see this entry in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And your unit, the military police company, would it have been aware or informed about this information when it arrived at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be by decision of the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would wish to object to the form of that question. I don't challenge the entry in the diary, but surely this witness, if he's going to be asked to comment on either material which relates to the diary or the diary itself, should be asked whether he actually been involved in its insertion of the material or whether he was aware of that particular entry. He's being asked for opinions that I would submit he can't possibly give. It's not his diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, what is there as your last question is really an assertion. And I think the point made by Mr. Moore is that you should commence with the question: "Were you or was your unit aware or informed about this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I showed the witness this excerpt from the war diary, I asked him whether he was informed about the announced arrival of the prisoners of war. But I can ask him again. It's not a problem. I put this other question because he already said in his previous answer that he was not informed. But here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you informed about this entry in the war diary from the 19th of November 1991 as the commander of the company of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you already that I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If the witness says no, what is the relevance of the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have resolved the matter now, gentlemen. And in any event we've reached the time for the break. Which we will now take and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I understand there's something you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. It's only a small matter. It's quite simply this: I did indicate to the Court that we would agree -- not that we can't disagree anyway, that we would proceed from 9.30 to 4.30 with variations perhaps on Monday and Friday. But it creates certain difficulties for our proofing because witnesses are coming in on certain days. We have a witness here, he is the next witness. I will finish today, I then will proceed proofing him this evening, and that creates its own difficulties administratively, and then I will have to try and proof him again. The most that I can do this evening is, I think, about two hours. I would merely ask if it is possible, for the Court to rise earlier tomorrow, or that the witness should not be called before Thursday. Under the old regime we could alternate if it was a morning or an afternoon, but the way the matters are at this time, I can't do it in the morning, it's not possible, because I deal with the witness who is already giving evidence, and in the evening there is a time restraint that's imposed because of WBSS, and actual physical ability to do so after a day in court. So I did indicate to the Court that I may make an application for an occasional period. This will be one. And then we have Vojnovic coming on Friday and I will be proofing him on Saturday and Sunday to commence on Monday. So I hope that that would be sufficient for him. But with regard to this witness, Vukosavljevic, I would ask that I be permitted to have a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do I see you with you at your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to support my learned friend from the Prosecution this time. For us it would be perfect so that we could have a good conversation with our clients tomorrow afternoon in the Detention Centre, so it would be a perfect opportunity for us for a longer consultation with our clients tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On this occasion we will not sit tomorrow beyond 12.30. If the present witness concludes before then, we will finish even earlier. That should assist in the particular interests and concerns of all counsel. It may even allow Mr. Lukic to have some fresh air and exercise. But don't take this as a general precedent for the pressures that counsel are under. If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit. Mr. Moore. Oh, sorry, Mr. Lukic. Let's try Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by the events that have just occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's hard on all of us, and perhaps that's just a reflection of that. But let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, when we stopped for the lunch break I asked you whether you knew about the entry from the war diary of the 80th Brigade of the 19th of November at 1800 hours, and you said that you didn't know about it. What I would like to ask you is the following: You were the commander of the military police company, so as part of your duties on the 18th and generally that a commander of a military police company would have, should you have been informed that the unit was to expect another group of prisoners of war that had to be guarded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken I tried to give you that answer before the break. This is something that is under the jurisdiction of the commander of the security sector. He is to decide on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 19th you came back from Sremska Mitrovica. I assume that was sometime in the late afternoon. What would I like to know is whether you reported to the security chief then, and did you inform him that you had completed your assignment in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I completed an assignment, because my unit was billeted to -- two houses away from the command post, so I would always stop by at the command post to see what was new and also to report on what had happened. During the day I would stop at the command post several times. On my return, I don't know if I stopped in at the command immediately, or after a while, I really -- I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to digress a little bit here. You said to my learned friend that on the 18th of November Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic introduced Captain Karanfilov to you and told you what his duties were in respect of the prisoners of war. Did you inform Vukosavljevic, your security organ, about that, or did he attend this meeting between yourself, Vojnovic and Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for sure is that the three of us talked and that there were some officers and soldiers around. I don't know exactly who was present. I can't remember. Because for me, what was important at that time was that I was given an assignment that I was expected to execute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And later did you inform your security chief that you were told that Captain Karanfilov was in charge of the prisoners of war or did you inform Jeftic about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragi Vukosavljevic was there, he was at Ovcara, you knew exactly the same things that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a question by my learned friend you said that on the 19th in the evening you went out on an assignment because of an incident. Did you return to the command post on the 19th or on the 20th, the command post of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, in the morning, can you tell us where you were and which assignments you had, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th on top of our regular duties we had received a request to secure and transport a group of officers who were supposed to go to Nijemci, amongst other places. Since I was not familiar with the terrain, and I could not issue an order and complete the procedure just by sending the driver, I sat with the driver and went to the field. We had maps that we used to orient ourselves and on the basis of which I issued various assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And was this a group of officers headed by the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though -- well, if the -- the clerks who were supposed to issue our salaries to us were under Danilovic, then yes, that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit 371? That would be the war diary of the 80th Brigade. And that would be the entry for the 20th of November at 8.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friends this is on page 10 of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 371, I think -- 371 we have is the exhibit for the operations diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm talking about the operations diary. There's obviously been a mistake in translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the 20th of November at 8.00, and it states there -- it's the 28th of November that we see here, but I would like to look at the entry of the 20th of November. I know the handwriting is a little bit unclear. Sir, you see this, 8.00, group of brigade officers, the following officers: Chief of Staff, operations assistant commander for moral guidance, two of the assistant commander for moral guidance assistant clerks went to Nemci in order to take stock of what the situation was in the unit that had taken part in the liberation of Podgradje village and Nemci village. Are we talk about the same group that you set out with on the 20th of November or this the same group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you understood me. The group that I was in charge of had received our salaries for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When was it that you set out with that group, roughly speaking, which time of day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this early in the morning. It was just before noon, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you left, who replaced you as company commander back in Negoslavci during your absence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer of the unit always did everything, and he knew what to do. So yes, he was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm asking too much, but do you remember who the duty officer was on this day in the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name, but if I may explain, my duty officer was always the same. But I can't remember his name. I only had two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And they took turns as duty officers, right, or were they duty officers at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about when the prison was set up. I broke my story there because I did not think that it was of interest to you. But I will try to explain now. This building that we used, the house, had two rooms where the soldiers slept. There was another room that I called the dining-room, there was a corridor where we kept the rifles and there was a basement. Up on the first floor I had the night-time observation post. In this room that I called the dining-room there was a table and a cupboard. Two soldiers were in charge of keeping this room squeaky-clean. Whenever soldiers returned from their mission, there always had to be something for them to eat or drink, so that they could rest afterwards. They made sure the room was clean and they made sure there was sufficient food as well as heating in that room. They worked 24-hour shifts in terms of their duty with the unit itself. I did not have any special duty officers taking turns or shifts because these two only looked after these assignments and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you returned from Nemci on the 20th, but you weren't sure about the time of day. Was it daylight, dusk, night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark by the time I reached Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Having reached Negoslavci, who did you go and report to, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my own unit, the duty officer told me that there was another security job for us, that a number of policemen had already left for Ovcara. I then joined the ones who were still there and we got into the vehicle. I'm not sure if I did or not, but most probably I did. I mean I did pass by the headquarters, I told them I was on my way. I can't remember who was there at the time. Probably because it was right near the house in which we were staying, that's why I can't remember. And we just drove straight on to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When the duty officer told you that the military police had already gone to Ovcara, did he inform you exactly who the officer was who went with this group? Your deputy, the company commander, who was in charge of this unit? Who led them in your absence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said there was a new security job for us to do, and that some men from our unit were there already. I have told you that I had a problem with manpower in terms of officers, and that was a problem that I faced in commanding my unit. I got into that vehicle and drove off to Ovcara. I didn't know who had taken the unit there or for what reason. All I knew was that there was another security job and that some elements of our unit were on it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say some elements of your unit were on it already. Does that mean that the rest of them were still back at the command post in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we have regular assignments. There were men going about the regular assignments already, some were with me and only those that were still left were involved. That's why I'm saying some elements. If you take into account the fact that a whole platoon was not there, then that would seem to imply that most of the unit was still stationary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps told if the traffic police platoon from your company secured the convoy that went to Ovcara on the 20th? I'm referring to the traffic police platoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I had was quite short. There was another security job, some parts of the unit were on this, and I was to go to Ovcara. I'm not sure if I've made this clear. I did not have sufficient men. I did not make any distinctions between paramedics, drivers, or policemen. I made no distinctions between the various types of soldiers. Simply because all who were there, all those who were available, had to carry out a military policeman's assignment. Other than that, as far as I know, no one from my unit was part of the security for this group. The first group or the second group. I'm sure about the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you set out for Ovcara to join the military policemen there, you stopped by the command post. Did the duty officer tell you if the other officers from the 80th Brigade were at Ovcara? Is this something you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell you or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at Ovcara on the 20th of November, you described what you found there. What I want to know is, did you see an officer from the 80th Brigade inside the hangar when you got there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of soldiers from our unit inside the hangar. Among others, a captain First Class, I think his name was Joca, the cafe owner in Kragujevac. He actually used to own a cafe in Kragujevac. He was there with part of his unit; some of his soldiers were there doing the same sort of disposition as everybody else. So when I came I ordered them all out of the hangar and he was one of those who left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this: Before you -- this person you say was called Joca Kafic left the hangar, was he perhaps involved in drawing up a list of the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was another soldier taking some notes. We were told that a list was being drawn up. At first I didn't really pay attention to this. I didn't ask myself any questions. They were making a list, apparently. Might be useful to them, I thought to myself. But I had been planning things the same way as on the previous occasion. I thought we should make a list during the night when everything settled. I wanted to have an A-4 sheet of paper and make copies knowing at this point in time what I would be facing the following morning. The fact that somebody else was drawing up a list there was not something that really caught my eye at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This fellow, Joca Kafic was he perhaps a reserve captain First Class from the 1st LAD PVO division whose commander was Jovan Macka [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He may well have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know about one particular unit of the 80th Motorised Brigade being the local command at Ovcara and being housed in a building about 200 or 300 metres away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know about the existence of any unit anywhere near that farm, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question, you're asking me if I knew about a command post of another unit being there. I did not know about that, but I did know about a unit being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thanks for clarifying that, sir. What sort of equipment did your signals officers have at Ovcara? Did your unit have any equipment, did any of the other unit commands have any equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we only had RUP 3 and RUP 12 because their batteries were in a poor state, these were not operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on this I am inclined to conclude that there was no communication between your unit and the other units. Do you know what the communication was like from the unit that was nearby, from their command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of equipment they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said that you had seen Joca Kafic inside the hangar. Was he the only officer from the 80th Brigade that you actually saw there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I spotted him. I don't remember spotting anybody else. Did you ever find out that the commander of the

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out that the commander of the 80th Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, on the 20th of November, 1991, at 1600 hours, had ordered the rotation of duty officers in order to watch the ZNG and MUP members and that he put the military police company and the brigade commanders in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You don't remember seeing any brigade command officers in the hangar, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what the lighting was like inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time around on the first security job that we had there, there was a generator and there were a handful of light bulbs inside the hangar. The lighting was poor, and inadequate. So both times I used additional light from the headlights of the Pinzgauers, which also had a search light mounted on it, so I used that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So under all this lighting you were eventually able to see clearly what was going on inside the hangar, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What mattered to me was to be able to see what was going on inside the hangar. To some extent anyway. The additional lighting I used was used outside the hangar but had no bearing on the light conditions inside the hangar. It was far from actually very good, but it was satisfactory under the conditions, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said you provided several statements in the past several years. In your testimony before the special court in Belgrade when testifying in the Ovcara case, in 2004, in October, do you remember having said that as of the moment of your arrival up to the moment when you withdrew, that everything on your part and the part of your unit that pertained to the hangar was done according to the rules and what you were taught professionally in various schools including the one in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to my learned friend, if transcripts are going to be put to the witness, in my submission it's only fair and proper that the witness should have an opportunity of having that before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, do you have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have that transcript. I just wanted to check with the witness whether he remembers having said that. In case he does, perhaps we needn't refer to the transcript, but in any case, I can give it to the witness with the usher's assistance. That is page 75. The date of the transcript is the 29th of October, 2004, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You have that portion highlighted. Did you find it? Could you please read it out for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: I think as of the moment of arrival until I went away that everything went according to the rules with what I had been taught in Bileca, Panco [as interpreted], et cetera, and in various other trainings before I withdrew."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state that before the Chamber in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters failed to catch the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I apologise, could you repeat your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what I have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in chief you said that once the order was established in the hangar that you allowed people to enter in small groups to see who was in the hangar. Did those groups contain one to three people, small numbers of people who entered and left the hangar and that there were no incidents during that time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the cursing and you have explained that our language abounds with swear words. What I wanted to ask is, these swear words that we use, would they raise any concern as regards anyone's security, or they are just another specific feature of the language we use?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to that. With all due respect for the Chamber and yourself, maybe we could discuss this somewhere else as regards this particular answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After having established order in the hangar, did everyone abide by your orders and the newly created situation and were there any problems prior to your unit pulling out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I conclude that you witnessed no maltreatment, beating or any type of physical assault against the detainees while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in chief you have explained the way you pulled out from Ovcara, and you said that you went back to the building where your unit was accommodated, is that correct, in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As regards the pulling out of your unit, did you report the security organ, in particular Drago [as interpreted] Vukosavljevic about that, be it that evening or the next morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragi Vukosavljevic, as far as I know, but I don't remember exactly, he was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dragi Vukosavljevic drafted a report concerning the events of the 20th of November at Ovcara and whether he forwarded that to the security department of the 1st Military District in Sid or to the 24th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you present at a meeting chaired by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic on the 21st of November where some of his subordinate officers were and the events of the 20th of November at Ovcara were discussed? Do you know of any such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present, and I don't know of any such a meeting. There were meetings, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next morning within the military police company, did you try to analyse your tasks on the 20th and did anyone from your unit report anything to you regarding that date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't conducted an analysis on the 19th or on the 20th -- 21st for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the 80th Brigade were you tasked, among other things, with the sanitation operation in the town of Vukovar to assist those people who came on behalf of the 1st Military District, including the military investigative representatives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the arrival at Vukovar, up until the moment I left, all that my unit could have done was beginning with the removing of bombs and explosives that we encountered often we had assistance from an engineering unit as well. We were tasked with securing the grammar school with the equipment that was there, we also had to secure a house close to the school which contained large quantities of explosives in the cellar. We also needed to secure the church. We had to intervene when fire broke out in the church and we were trying to save the Catholic library there. We had to intervene whenever we were told a corpse was found. We had to secure the scene until the people who would clear it up arrived. I'm trying to remember what else we were tasked with, but this was quite comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the duties of your unit in the sanitisation plan, apart from the military investigative organs were there also civilian investigative organs included? I have in mind the civilian magistrate from civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I helped the police unit to be formed that spent a few days in the barracks and then they were billeted elsewhere. We cooperated with civilian authorities. I cooperated with the TO command as well as with the civilian police when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were within a military company -- military police company, did you know that on the 22nd of November the 80th Brigade took over the area of responsibility that used to belong to the Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such matters were of no importance to me. I didn't need to know whether it was OG South or the 80th Brigade command or someone else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take your official notebook? Perhaps we could clarify a couple of things. Page 64. The date is the 20th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what there is just below the date, because I can't read that out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Patrol all the way up to Sotin." Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In Slavkamenac [phoen], Major Dragotinovic [phoen], Major Jankovic, Lieutenant Danilovic, and the security organ, the organ for morale security Tovarnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this an entry pertaining to the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what this entry means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patrol up to Sotin, that means that I sent one of my patrols to go as far as Sotin, and the rest I don't know. It doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 65, which is the next page, contains some names. Do the names pertain to the 20th of November, and do they mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and this is not even my handwriting. It means that someone else made this entry, I must have given the notebook to someone and then they made the entry. It's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go to page 66. At the top there is a name. Nikola Plavic [as interpreted], does that mean anything to you, is that your handwriting, and do you remember when that was written?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the entry below, could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The centre for collection and accommodation of civilians and material property. Captain First Class Antic Kresojevic and Stojanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A correction for the transcript. Could you please read it out again slowly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither of the entries mean anything to mean. The first one reads "Nikola Plavsic, son of Nikola, the 27th of May 1933, Vukovar. Franciceva Street number 10, Vukovar." Below the line the centre for accommodation of civilians and taking care of material property. Below that commander Ljubinko Stojanovic, Captain First Class commander of the rear unit, Antic Kresojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said these entries mean nothing to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 68, if you continue with the previous page, the 67th, that pertains to the 24th of November; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. Because the 24th the entries there, that's not my signature, so I must have given the notebook to someone to write something down. Should I read out what it states on page 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. I'm going to ask you about some entries. All I was asking you was when you give your notebook for somebody to write something down, is that all in the course of the line of duty? What does it mean when you give it -- your notebook to somebody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that I probably gave it to some of my soldiers, so that I could perhaps do something else in that time. Then I would ask some of them perhaps to note something down for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please now read the entry on page 68, and could you please check when the entry was made?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zavisic, commander of the police station --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully submit that it might be prudent to clarify with regard to each witness, whether this witness has actually written that page, and whether he's aware of the content and agree with it, rather than get him to read it as such. Those preliminary steps may assist everyone, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the witness answered all these matters when he didn't write something or when he doesn't know something. So I think that the witness actually responded in each case in terms of what my learned friend has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you write this entry on page 68, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matters, if you wouldn't mind if you are asked to refer to and read an entry in the diary, which is not your entry, would you say so at the beginning? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states on page 68, Zavisic, and then there is an asterisk, commander of the police station in Vukovar, Zavisic Miodrag. Underneath that it says SO Slavonia, Baranja and western Srem, Dragan Djukic, station commander. Branko Obradovic, police chief. Bogunovic, internal affairs minister. I wrote this down, and the date is something that I cannot remember, but it's probably somewhere around the 27th when I said the civilian police was established. So at that point that was probably the composition of that police force in terms of a particular command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Borivoje Borovic, and I represent Miroslav Radic. First let us clarify. How many people did you definitely have in your company when you came to the area of Vukovar? Is that the number, 60, including the drivers, officers, medical staff and the auxiliary staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Smederevo where I was with a number of police officers, one platoon was taken away. So I came to Negoslavci perhaps with 25 to 30 policemen, and I can check this in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, as part of that company, did you have any auxiliary staff, drivers, medics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who responded to the call-up were present. I cannot really tell you exactly how many of each type of personnel there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many people did you have in the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example in Negoslavci it was around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were guarding the first group at Ovcara, how many soldiers did you have who carried out this guard duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20 military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second time when you were guarding on the 20th of November at Ovcara, how many policemen did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably similar. Between 15 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The first time, was it enough to have 20 people to be able to carry out the assignment of guarding that first group at Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I had about 60 people who were carrying out the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get those 60 policemen the first time, where did they go to for the second time, the following day? Why didn't you have 60 policemen the following day as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness didn't say that he had 60 policemen, he had said that he had 60 people. And indeed he had actually said earlier on it was 20 military policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must say that's a distinction I hadn't appreciated, Mr. Moore. My understanding was the same as Mr. Borovic's. But it can be made clear by Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not being clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go again. The first time when you were securing the Mitnica group, you had 20 military policemen. Who did you command on top of that, which other group that was also securing the Mitnica group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already said that, but I will repeat it. Besides the policemen in the security of the first group, there were also officers there from the 80th Motorised Brigade, and also a certain number of soldiers from other units that the commander, Vojnovic, redirected to guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these soldiers from the 80th Kragujevac Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November was it enough to have just your 20 military policemen to completely execute the task that you were given, was that enough people to do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th I did establish order with that number of people. But it would have been very -- to do this the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well this is a different question. Let's go --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this. There was a question that was asked quite specifically, Mr. Borovic wasn't getting the answer that he wanted and he interrupted the witness. The witness should be allowed to answer the question properly. If my learned friend Mr. Borovic doesn't like it, he can live with it and afterwards and other questions [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be good if we calm down, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will put it as politely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be enough, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovic, if you would be good enough to let the witness answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question was, was 20 military policemen enough to establish order and to execute the assignment that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to answer. I did establish order with that number of people. However, to work the whole night with that number of people would have been too exhausting and it was a question if everything would have been done according to all the elements that needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you do anything in terms of informing Vojnovic to again assign soldiers to you who would, just like the first time, guard the detained persons in shifts, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you permit me, I cannot just answer with a yes or a no. Because I am trying to explain to you that at that point when I arrived I did establish order, everything was proceeding in a regular manner, then there was the command that I should withdraw or pull out. So I did not manage to carry out all the actions that I was planning to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just am going to tell you the following: You did not spend 15 minutes there, we're gradually going to establish how long you spent there. First of all, to clarify the circumstances, how much time did you need to get to Negoslavci from Sremska Mitrovica by car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Second question, how many kilometres is it in your assessment from Sremska Mitrovica to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it then, and I don't know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Third question, if I was to tell you this was less than 50 kilometres, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time is needed to cover 50 kilometres by car for you? In terms of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you usually drive so slowly, 50 an hour on the motorway? All right. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something? Which motorway? There is no motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. I accept the answer. One hour.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've already provided a statement to the investigators of the OTP. It's on page 9. Do you have that statement? If not, I can read it to you. On page 9 you say that you left Sremska Mitrovica and then the next sentence is, "When I came back I was informed that some of my military policemen were again sent to Ovcara to secure or guard a second group of prisoners, so that I immediately," I emphasise immediately, "went there." Is this what you told the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what it says in that passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well then I don't know what is not correct there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm that this is what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that on page 9 it says that you returned from Sremska Mitrovica at about 1600 hours -- no, I apologise, that you left Sremska Mitrovica at around 1600 hours, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make a pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please kindly estimate how many kilometres was it from Negoslavci to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say it was three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Line 74 -- page 74, line 7, it's written down as probably, but the witness said "certainly."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted what you read, but the word "verovatno" probably was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry, what did you say about the distance from Negoslavci to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say it was three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long would it take you to cover that stretch of three kilometres in a Pinzgauer, in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 10 minutes, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we have now established that you left Sremska Mitrovica at 1600 hours, then you had to have been at Ovcara at 1500 hours and 10 minutes [as interpreted]. Do we agree based on my mathematics that we have come to, and that we have calculated?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, there is a transcript -- a mistake in the transcript. It should have stated 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this would have to be 1700 hours and 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have taken a -- a theoretical approach according to which, once I turned on the ignition of my vehicle from Sremska Mitrovica I just drove without stopping and then I came to Negoslavci. That's the theory. But what's actually was the real situation and what happened to me on the road is that possibly I could have reached Ovcara one and a half hours later, but it's possible that I arrived at Ovcara sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I really don't remember when I exactly came to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us accept that it was perhaps an hour and a half later after leaving Sremska Mitrovica, so it must have been 1700 hours 30 at the most, it's November, it's winter, and it gets dark quite early; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If the war diary of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade says that you pulled out on -- at 2230 hours, how many hours is that that you spent in Ovcara performing your duties as a military policeman, can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it says in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I were to tell you that it says in the war diary, and I want to be quite fair, that you pulled out at 2230 hours, doesn't that not come to four hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it say there that I pulled out at 2230 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The military police company.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I pulled out at 2230 hours, well, that means -- I'm just thinking aloud, because I don't know. All I know is that I came, I was there for some time, and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's finish with this topic. I tried carefully, question by question, to show that you spent about four hours there, it wasn't such a short period of time, not that you just came and left. You came, established order, and left. This is something we will evaluate through other witnesses and on the basis of what you said. So I would like to then push ahead. Where was your deputy from, because you are obviously avoiding to say his name. Did you have one deputy or several deputies in the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the person who was the deputy in terms of the establishment ever responded to the call-up to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question. In your absence, who would have deputised for you and commanded the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the duty officer would take over every time I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who commanded your company, the element of your company that was at Ovcara while you were in Sremska Mitrovica and who met you there when you returned at 1630 hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That last part of the question is clearly not what the witness said was the time, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Defence -- my apologies 1730, my mistake. I apologise. I apologise. The mistake is mine. 1730.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will start with the last part of your question. I'm not sure when I got there. That's the first thing. Secondly, I don't know who raised the unit. I don't know who was in charge of unit because I wasn't he there, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But when you were in Ovcara, who was in command of your unit before you returned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there was no command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have Exhibit 256 on our screens, page 22, specifically. Page 22 is what I need. Thank you. This environment shown in the photograph, does that ring a bell, is that familiar? Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the usher could please hand you a pen, and could you please use that pen to indicate the hangar where you, as you say, established order on the 20th of November. Can you mark that as number 1, please, and circle it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 2, to indicate the spot where the guards were staying, the room where they were resting, this other group who was waiting for the security men.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I comment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mark first, then comment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were considering the possibility of putting the reserve men there, but it was a very cold spot and was not convenient at all. So I took my policemen inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark with number 3 the outer ring of security, as you called it. Could you please draw the outer ring and mark it as number 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please indicate where the Pinzgauers were that were providing additional lighting for the hangar. Where were they parked? Number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an overlap here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Use an arrow to get out of that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please use an arrow to indicate the direction of the yellow house that you referred to from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was this way. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this photograph into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could something be clarified, please, Mr. Borovic? Perhaps the witness might help me. The number 3, the outer ring of security, you seem to have just indicated one position. Did you have guards posted around the hangar on the outside, or were they only located in one position at the -- about the door, as you have arrowed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They weren't all around the building, they were along the stretch between the door and to the right, based on this photograph. That was the movement of the guards. Towards the yellow house, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you had no security on the ends or the back of the hangar at all on the outside? And how many guards did you have on the outside? I accepted your nodding of the head as indicating your answer was no. You had no security other than near the hangar door. If that is correct, how many guards did you use outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my estimate, the guards should have provided security and monitored any vehicles coming from the direction of the yellow house. I do not believe that anyone could have approached the area from the opposite direction, not in a vehicle anyway. And there was hardly any danger of anyone walking up to us. So I placed my guard outside the door and he was moving to the right. Based on this photograph. One or two guards, when in there was a visit, there would be two. When there was no visit, there would be one, or at least that's how it turned out to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, Mr. Borovic; I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, this has been of great assistance. I would like to wrap this up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many doors does this hangar have, entrances, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the one that we used to get in at the back there's -- what should I call it, at the opposite end there's another entrance as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone securing that rear entrance or exit, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've just tried to explain that using the map. I didn't think there was any danger, any potential danger, from that side, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just another question. I'm wrapping up this set of questions now, since it's time for a break. Were only soldiers from your military police company securing the main entrance and no one else? Were they only men from your company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At no point in time were the men from my company the only ones providing the security, but rather people from the 80th Motorised Brigade taking shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many other men from the 80th Motorised Brigade were there in addition to your own military police company on the 20th of November? You say they were taking turns or taking shifts in cooperation from with soldiers from the 80th Motorised Brigade, the Kragujevac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph that you showed me, that was in relation to the 18th and 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about that at all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was telling you all of this in relation to the 18th and the 19th. The last thing you asked still stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Hold on there. This is the witness's understanding, that this was in relation to the 18th of November. May that be noted. Although that wasn't what I was asking him about. And then we can ask him again about the 20th under a different set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a convenient time for us to have a break, Your Honours. And I seek that this be admitted into evidence as showing the situation on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to mark it with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you would prefer to clear up the situation on the 20th after the break, Mr. Borovic? We will adjourn now to 20 past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, Ovcara was -- thank you. Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November Vojnovic and you chose Ovcara as the location for the detention unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was this meant to be a detention unit used for all future prisoners in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our assignment was to find a building that met all the criteria for guarding POWs. That was our assignment and that was what we did. As for any future prisoners, that wasn't something that I knew at the time. If you're asking me about whether this was to become a permanent facility --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming the war had gone on for another three years or so, then that could have been the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the more serious side, or let's try to make this answer of yours more serious. On the 18th of November were you building a permanent detention unit that was to be there for as long as you stayed in Vukovar, not knowing at that time how soon you would be leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Negoslavci, yes? It wasn't in Vukovar, it was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does that mean that on the 19th and 20th of November you had a regular detention unit in Negoslavci or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony you explained the situation at Ovcara on the 18th of November. Can we please have Exhibit 256, page 22, displayed again? Page 22. That's it. Thank you. Sir, now about the 20th of November, 1991, could you please mark the spot where the outer ring of security was that you referred to in your earlier evidence as existing on the 20th of November? And please mark that with number 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard was outside the door on the 20th of November. [Marks] Like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you had no outer ring at all? There was a single guard, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely established order, and started the security job. I had not yet completed or finished the job in the proper sense of the word. The situation I found when I came was sorted out. By now, with the exception of the military policemen and the detainees, there was nobody else inside the hangar. The rope was pulled up, there was a guard, a military policeman standing outside the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've heard about that. Thank you. Can you please mark the spot where the Pinzgauers were and how many were there outside the hangar? Can you draw that for us please, use a line, a dotted line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember their exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you did tell us, didn't you, that you used the headlights of those vehicles to light the interior of the hangar. Where were these vehicles then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used a Pinzgauer that was parked just outside the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that, please, just the location. You see that you can.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many soldiers, military policemen from your company were inside at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20, I reckon. More like 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Joca Kafic, how many of his own soldiers were this whom you ordered to leave the hangar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where did those men go next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many were there to begin with and I have no idea where they went afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours I seek that this be admitted into evidence. Having in mind what the witness marked am in relation to the 18th of November, I don't we will be needing this for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 434, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Joca Kafic, commanded his own group, and then you sent them away. How did you know that he was the commander of a group? Did you know that previously before you arrived, or did you just realise on the spot?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Joca was a captain first class by rank. There were a number of his soldiers there. At one point I said that all those who were not military police officers should go out and they obeyed. They left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were there 10 of those or more than 10?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now go back to that question which you failed to answer right at the outset. Had it been necessary for you to stay until the next day, would it have been sufficient for you to call Vojnovic and ask him again to send over his soldiers who would then take turns guarding the hangar throughout the night? Would that have been a way to do it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I'm certain about is that had I continued with the security job, I would have got more soldiers to help out with it throughout the night, just as the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You set up the rope for the first time on the 18th of November. The other thing you did is you drew up a list. The second time around on the 20th of November, you applied a procedure which is more or less the same again, you set up this rope down the middle of the hangar, you guard the prisoners, and what do you do next? Do you start drawing up lists, or were you not thinking about the list at all at this point in time? Or rather, was it possible that Joca Kafic, his real name was Jovan Novakovic, right, had already drawn up a list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I start at the end. Joca was making up a list wit a soldier there. I'm not sure what became of it eventually. As for my own actions once order had been established and the soldiers were standing to the right of the door and the rope was to the right of the door, and not down the middle of the hangar. When only military policemen were inside the hangar, in addition to the prisoners of course, I started allowing other people into the building too. Those who wanted to go around the rope to see who was inside. They would come in, and they would then leave. It was of paramount importance for me, given the fact that the situation had been a total mess before and was now, eventually, under the control of the military police, to keep things this way, to keep things under control. But I was already thinking about calling in the reinforcements I was already thinking about having more soldiers come over to help us out. I was thinking about getting some more food. I was thinking about getting some more water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. We've covered that before. My question is, under just which military rule is it that you allowed members of the TO into this hangar guarded by your military policemen, knowing that they would mistreat prisoners once inside? On the other hand, you had sent away soldiers belonging to Ovcara's local command, who had been there all along before you arrived. Don't you think that you -- you may thereby have violated the rules governing the conduct of a military police commander, once you allowed these people inside to take a look? What was the reason you believed it necessary to allow them in so that they could have a look?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three questions, a total of three questions, if I follow. There are three questions for me to answer, right? The first question being those people who came in did not mistreat anyone. Nor did they attack anyone. The prisoners, specifically. Secondly, it was my personal assessment as the commander that the safest thing for the prisoners and for the whole security job was to allow the TO men to have a look at the people who were there. Thirdly I'm not sure what your third question was, I've lost track, sorry. Oh, right, yes. Under which rule I could have done this. It was a matter of my personal assessment, I believed this to be the safest option for the task in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you've answered this one to some extent already, but does that mean you had full control of the detention unit? When I say under control, I mean the safety of the prisoners and I mean keeping at bay, so to speak, the TO men. Both these things, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, that's why my answer is delayed. I'm certain that I had full control of the prisoners' security at this time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question, you were there with the brigade commander Vojnovic you are looking for a location to receive a large number of people. Did he explain to you about the unit that was actually there? That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic must have told me about the adjacent units, or unit. I'm not sure exactly what he told me, but when you asked me the three questions earlier on, I think you also said this: You said that I had sent those soldiers away.
